memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'You have saved our lives,' they said. 'May we find favour in the eyes of our lord; we will be in bondage to Pharaoh.' So Joseph established it as a law concerning land in Egypt—still in force today—that a fifth of the produce belongs to Pharaoh. It was only the land of the priests that did not become Pharaoh's." — Gen 47:25-26 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
"You have saved our lives." That is the people's own verdict on Joseph, and it should shape how we read this whole section. They are not bitter. They are grateful. They know that without him, they and their children would be dead.

Whatever the hard economics of it, the people who lived through it called it salvation.

And here is a thought worth sitting with. The man who saved Egypt was the one Egypt had imprisoned. He had been a foreign slave, wrongly accused, forgotten in a cell. The nation's rescuer came up out of a dungeon.

God does this repeatedly. The rejected one becomes the deliverer. The stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone (Ps 118:22; Acts 4:11). Joseph's story is a faint rehearsal of a far greater one: a man handed over by his own people, condemned, put in the ground — and raised up to become the salvation of the very people who rejected Him.

The Egyptians said, "You have saved our lives," to a former prisoner. One day every knee will bow to a crucified Saviour (Phil 2:10-11).

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. What has God brought out of a season when you felt forgotten?
2. How does Joseph's path from prison to rescuer point you to Christ?
3. Have you personally said to Jesus, "You have saved my life"?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord Jesus, You were rejected and condemned, and You became the salvation of the world. Thank You for saving my life. Let my whole life say so. Amen.
